FGCU QUANTUM HACKATHON, IBM QISKIT FALL FEST 2026

Rewind and Amplify: the results

We fused Grover’s algorithm with a quantum recurrent state machine, the model from our hidden-defect project. It didn’t bolt on, and noise punishes it. So we redesigned it around noise. This page is what we found, including what we got wrong.

@@GAIN@@fewer machine calls to condition on a real 64-step record, most of it from steering
@@GATES@@fewer two-qubit gates than textbook Grover, with better answers on five IBM device models
@@SEP@@clearer separation of a hidden defect from none, at equal shots
@@HWFIRSTR@@chance of a rare event on a real IBM chip with 40 gates, against @@HWFIRSTB@@ for textbook Grover with 213

The problem

The most useful events in a quantum system are often rare. Our model only generates, so asking “what happens around this rare event?” means running it and throwing away every run that doesn’t match. Matching one real 64-step click record takes about 27 million runs. Grover’s algorithm promises the square root of that, but it has to run the machine backwards, and the machine resets a qubit every step. You can’t Grover what you can’t rewind.

Four moves

1. PurifyA fresh qubit replaces every reset. The run becomes one reversible circuit that holds every click history at once.
2. SteerTune one gate so the event is common. Part of the rarity disappears for free, and conditional answers stay exact.
3. Amplify locallyOne iteration, with a reflection on 3 qubits at any record length.
4. VerifyThe event is measured, so a failed shot shows itself and is dropped.

It works exactly

Purifying changes nothing: amplitudes match the exact model to @@AMP@@, and the two circuits click alike over a million shots each. Then Qiskit’s own Grover operator follows the textbook curve on the machine’s histories, within @@CURVE@@ on six questions.

What it costs

Scaling follows theory: the log-log slope is −0.50 against −1.00 for plain sampling, out to one-in-a-million events. With p unknown, the standard schedule costs about twice as much and still scales as the square root.

For a real 64-step record, steering every clicked step takes 27.5 million runs down to 6,240. Grover then takes that to 125 calls. Steering is classical importance sampling, and it does most of the work: about 4,400 times, against about 50 times from Grover.

Resilience under noise

We tested on five IBM device snapshots, none of them the one we developed the idea on. Each circuit was compiled for the device and simulated with its noise model.

A cheaper, slightly approximate circuit beats the exact one, because the error it adds is smaller than the noise it avoids.

The reflection we got wrong first

Our first shortcut watched only the two memory qubits. The hit rate looked fine. Then a harder test showed it scrambled the hidden state: with no defect, the clicks after a click came out as [0.091, 0.029, 0.009] where the truth is [0.018, 0.058, 0.101]. Hit rate alone would never have shown that. The maths pointed at the fix, which is to watch the light the question reads as well.

What it can answer

A physics question: what happens right after a rare click? With no defect, a click wipes the machine, so what follows simply restarts the run. A hidden defect remembers across the click. That’s a fingerprint of hidden memory, and you can only read it by conditioning. So we amplify the click and keep running the machine: Grover inside the recurrent loop.

The other slot: a QRSM as the oracle

Grover has two slots: what to search, and what counts as a match. Timofey’s idea fills the second. A reader QRSM reads a vague request token by token, turning the phase of each entry that matches. It found the right table for 19 of 20 vague requests.

This shows the architecture and no more. The oracle is compiled from the catalogue, so classical code has already read every entry: 1,024 entries takes 32,800 two-qubit gates, against a 1,024-step scan.

On real IBM chips

On 5 November 2026 we ran the same 39 circuits on two 156-qubit IBM chips: @@HWJOBS@@ jobs, @@HWSECONDS@@ seconds of device time, at most 11 qubits per circuit. We committed our predictions first.

On ibm_kingston, steer + local won @@HWWINS@@ comparisons across five jobs. The chip punished depth about 3 times harder per gate than its noise model said, so the lead came out about twice what simulation predicted.

The fingerprint came through. Telling a defect from none reached @@HWZFIRST@@ and @@HWZAGAIN@@ standard errors on Kingston, and @@HWZMOVED@@ on Marrakesh, where plain sampling never passed 2. It’s fragile: dynamical decoupling erased it. We predicted twirling would, and we were wrong.

Calibration hid a bad patch. On Marrakesh, the compiler chose the qubits that looked best in the calibration data, and they did far worse than the others we used: @@HWBADECHO@@ error per gate, against about 0.2% reported. Our echo circuits caught it. Moving off those five qubits recovered the result. We picked them after seeing the data, so that job tests the explanation, and it isn’t a clean replication.

What we don’t claim

  • No speedup. An exact classical sampler gives a sample in about a millisecond here. Its cost grew about 6 times per hidden qubit, so a crossover is plausible but not shown.
  • Small hardware runs. @@HWJOBS@@ jobs on two chips in one evening, at most 11 qubits and 5 steps. Everything else here is simulation, including the IBM noise models.
  • No rewinding of real chips. We rewind a model learned from clicks. A physical defect can’t be run backwards.
  • Steering is classical. It is exact only for clicks at known steps, and needs a rough value of p.
  • The local reflection is an approximation. Steered, its hit rate falls to 0.73 at T = 14.
  • The core idea isn’t new. Amplified rejection sampling goes back to Low, Yoder and Chuang (2014). Ours is the mapping onto hidden quantum models, and the resilience work.

Why it could matter

Conditioning on a 64-step record takes about 2.7 million gates as textbook Grover, and about 40,000 once steered. IBM’s published 2029 target of 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates would, by our rough estimate, fit a machine with 50 hidden qubits and a 150-step record, whose memory alone would take about 18 petabytes classically. That is where our classical baseline stops working.
